source_text: Χρὴ δὲ ἔτι νέον ὄντα φοβεῖσθαι Θεὸν, πρὶν ἢ ἑαυτὸν παραδοῦναι κακοῖς, πρὶν ἐλθεῖν τὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ μεγάλην ἡμέραν καὶ φοβερὰν, ὁπότε ἥλιος μὲν οὐκέτι λάμψει, οὐδὲ σελήνη, οὐδὲ οἱ λοιποὶ ἀστέρες, κινηθήσονται δὲ αἱ ὑπέρτεραι δυνάμεις, ἐν ἐκείνῳ τῷ ὅλων χειμῶνι καὶ ταράχῳ, οἱ κοσμοφύλακες ἄγγελοι· ὡς παύσασθαι μὲν ἄνδρας δυνάστας, παύσασθαι δὲ καὶ γυναῖκας ἐργαζομένας, φευγούσας εἰς τὰ σκοτεινὰ τῶν οἰκημάτων, κεκλεισμένων ἁπασῶν τῶν θυρῶν· καί τις γυνὴ τοῦ ἀλήθειν ἀποσχομένη διὰ τὸ δέος, ἰσχνοτάτῃ φωνῇ χρήσεται ὥσπερ λεπτότατον ὄρνεον· ἅπασαι δὲ ἄναγνοι γυναῖκες εἰς γῆν πεσοῦνται, καὶ πόλεις καὶ αἱ τούτων ἀρχαὶ αἱ μιαιφόνοι, περιμένουσαι τὴν ἄνωθεν κόλασιν, ἐνστάντος καιροῦ πικροτάτου καὶ αἱματώδους, ὥσπερ ἀνθοῦντος ἀμυγδάλου καὶ συνεχῶν ἐπικειμένων κολάσεων, ὥσπερ πλήθους ἐφιπταμένων ἀκρίδων, καὶ ἐκποδῶν ῥιπτουμένων τῶν παρανόμων, ὥσπερ μελαίνης καὶ εὐκαταφρονήτου καππάρεως. Καὶ ὁ μὲν ἀγαθὸς ἀνὴρ εἰς αἰώνιον οἶκον τὸν ἑαυτοῦ χαίρων πορεύσεται· οἱ δέ γε φαῦλοι, πάντα τὰ αὐτῶν ἐμπλήσουσι κοπτόμενοι, καὶ οὔτε ἀργύριον ἀποτεθησαυρισμένον, οὔτε χρυσίον δόκιμον ἐπωφελὲς ἔτι. Μεγάλη γὰρ ἅπαντα καθέξει πληγὴ, καὶ μέχρις ὑδρίας ἑστώσης πρός τινι κρήνῃ, καὶ τροχοῦ ὀχήματος, ὃν ἂν τύχῃ καταλελεῖφθαι ἐν τῷ κοιλώματι παυσαμένης, χρόνον τε περιδρομῆς, καὶ τῆς δι᾽ ὕδατος ζωῆς παροδεύσαντος τοῦ λουτροφόρου αἰῶνος. Ἀνθρώπων δὲ ἐπὶ γῆς κειμένων μία σωτηρία, εἰ ἐπιγνοῖεν αὐτῶν αἱ ψυχαὶ, καὶ πρὸς αὐτὸν ἀναπταῖεν ὑφ᾽ οὗ καὶ γεγέννηνται.
thought_title: Fear God before the great and terrible day
orientation: Fear God while young, before the great and terrible day when the heavens are shaken and the wicked are punished.
pass_a_gloss: It is necessary while still being young to fear God, before giving over oneself to evils, before there comes the great and fearful day of God, when the sun will no longer shine, nor the moon, nor the remaining stars, and the higher powers will be moved in that storm and turmoil of all things, the world-guarding angels; so that powerful men cease, and also working women cease, fleeing into the dark parts of the dwellings, all the doors having been shut; and some woman having abstained from grinding through fear will use a most thin voice like a most slender bird; and all impure women will fall to earth, and cities and their bloodstained governments, awaiting the punishment from above, a most bitter and bloody season having set in, like an almond flowering, and continual punishments pressing on, like a multitude of locusts flying upon, and the lawless being hurled out of the way, like a black and contemptible caper. And the good man will go rejoicing into his own eternal house; but the base will fill all their things beating their breasts, and neither silver stored up nor approved gold is any longer beneficial. For a great blow will hold fast all things, even as far as a water jar standing at some spring, and a wheel of a vehicle which may happen to have been left in the hollow, the washing-bringing age having passed by the time both of the circuit having ceased and of the life through water. For humans lying upon earth one salvation: if their souls should recognize and fly up to Him by whom they also have been begotten.

pass_b_english: One must fear God while still young (Ecclesiastes 12:1), before giving oneself over to evils, before the great and terrible day of God comes, when the sun will shine no more, nor the moon, nor the rest of the stars (Ecclesiastes 12:2; Matthew 24:29), and the higher powers, the angels who guard the world, will be shaken in that storm and turmoil of all things (Ecclesiastes 12:3). So men of power will cease, and the women at their work will cease too (Ecclesiastes 12:3), fleeing into the dark corners of the houses with all the doors shut (Ecclesiastes 12:4). A woman who has stopped grinding for fear will speak in the faintest voice, like the smallest bird (Ecclesiastes 12:4). All the impure women will fall to the ground (Ecclesiastes 12:4), and so will cities and their bloodstained governments, as they await the punishment from above, when a most bitter and bloody season has set in, like an almond tree in flower, when punishments press on without pause, like a swarm of locusts flying down, and when the lawless are flung out of the way like a black and worthless caper bush (Ecclesiastes 12:5).

The good man will go rejoicing to his own eternal home; but the wicked will fill all that is theirs with beating of breasts (Ecclesiastes 12:5), and neither silver laid up in store nor tested gold will be of use any longer (Ecclesiastes 12:6). For a great blow will seize everything, even down to the jar standing at a spring, and the wheel of a carriage that happens to have been left in the hollow (Ecclesiastes 12:6), when the age that brings the washing has passed beyond the time of the circling, now at an end, and of the life given through water.
For human beings who lie upon the earth there is one salvation: that their souls come to know Him by whom they were begotten, and fly up to Him (Ecclesiastes 12:7).
notes: Metaphrase of Ecclesiastes 12:1-7, read as the last day. Reads ἔτι and τὰ as corrected in the source row. Matthew 24:29 is cited beside the sun, moon and stars because Gregory joins the darkened lights to the shaking of the heavenly powers, as in that verse. 'The great and terrible day' also echoes Joel 2:31 and Malachi 4:5, but the Greek wording (φοβεράν) does not match the LXX (ἐπιφανῆ), so those are left uncited. 'The angels who guard the world' stands in apposition to 'the higher powers' and is Gregory's reading of 'the keepers of the house' (Ecclesiastes 12:3). 'Bloodstained governments' renders αἱ ἀρχαὶ αἱ μιαιφόνοι. 'Caper bush' renders κάππαρις (LXX Ecclesiastes 12:5). 'Beating of breasts' renders κοπτόμενοι (Ecclesiastes 12:5, the mourners). Doubtful: the sentence on the jar and the wheel is compressed. The English follows the print without emendation: χρόνον is the object of παροδεύσαντος in the genitive absolute ('when the age that brings the washing has passed beyond the time of the circling ... and of the life given through water'), as the 1622 Latin construes it ('ablutionem ferente seculo tum conuersionis atque iactationis, tum eius vitae quae per aquam comparatur, tempus praetergresso'). παυσαμένης (feminine genitive) is taken with περιδρομῆς ('the circling, now at an end'); the Latin passes over it. 'In the hollow' renders ἐν τῷ κοιλώματι; 'cistern' (LXX λάκκος) is not added. The 1622 Latin takes 'the age that brings the washing' (λουτροφόρου αἰῶνος) of baptism; the English keeps the literal image and does not add the word baptism. 'Begotten' keeps γεγέννηνται (have been begotten/born); Gregory's form of Ecclesiastes 12:7 (the spirit returns to God who gave it). No Psalm citations.
